group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 75-year-old man was brought to the emergency department just after noon by staff from the skilled-nursing facility where he has resided for the past two years because of progressive osteoarthritis and mobility limitations but otherwise manages his own finances and medications; the on-site licensed practical nurse became concerned when he developed a new cough and noticeably rapid breathing during the morning medication pass. According to the transfer sheet, the cough began three days ago as a scant dry irritation but overnight turned wetter, yielding small amounts of rust-tinged sputum with each effort, and this morning the patient complained that “my right side feels heavy when I breathe in.” He denied chills, rigors, or pleuritic chest pain, and an axillary temperature recorded at the facility peaked at 99.5 °F two hours before transport. His medical history is remarkable for child-Pugh A alcoholic cirrhosis discovered eight years earlier after evaluation for thrombocytopenia; he completed a structured abstinence program and has required no paracentesis, no encephalopathy treatment, and maintains normal synthetic function on laboratory surveillance. He has never been told he has chronic kidney disease, heart muscle weakness, prior transient ischemic attacks, or any form of cancer, and the last comprehensive metabolic panel faxed from his primary care visit six months ago showed a serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. He quit smoking three decades ago after a 20-pack-year exposure, drinks only coffee, and has never used illicit drugs. Immunizations are current except he declined the most recent seasonal influenza vaccine because of scheduling conflicts with facility transportation. The nursing staff withheld antipyretics, inhalers, supplemental oxygen, and intravenous fluids so that hospital clinicians could obtain baseline measurements. On arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, conversed appropriately with the triage nurse, correctly identified the date and location, and followed multi-step commands without hesitation. Skin appeared lightly flushed but dry, and capillary refill was less than two seconds. Pre-intervention vital signs were: oral temperature 99.5 °F, heart rate 126 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, automated blood pressure 106/58 mm Hg confirmed by manual reading, respiratory rate 50 breaths per minute with shallow excursions and mild intercostal retraction, and fingertip pulse oximetry 91 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude. Neck veins were not distended, and there was no peripheral edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung examination disclosed markedly decreased breath sounds at the right base with stony dullness to percussion and faint egophony just above the area, while the left lung carried coarse inspiratory crackles scattered posteriorly. The abdomen was soft and nontender; the liver edge was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin with a firm, nodular contour but no obvious ascites. Neurologic screening showed equal and reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, symmetric facial expression, and 5/5 strength in all extremities; finger-to-nose testing was smooth, and gait was not assessed because of baseline mobility limitations. A bedside capillary glucose measured 137 mg/dL. Venous blood was drawn, and an arterial sample from the left radial artery was obtained within ten minutes of arrival before any therapy. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 117 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 92 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 50 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, the latter only slightly above his outpatient baseline. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 14.8 × 10⁹/L with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 60 %, hemoglobin 20.1 g/dL, and platelets 110 × 10⁹/L. The arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated pH 7.23, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, PaO₂ 87 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation and mild hypoxemia. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any medications or fluids revealed a dense consolidation involving the right middle and lower lobes accompanied by a curvilinear meniscus blunting the right costophrenic angle, suggesting a moderate pleural fluid collection; the cardiac silhouette and mediastinum were within normal limits for age, and the left lung fields were clear aside from minimal dependent atelectasis. Electrocardiography performed concurrently showed sinus tachycardia at 125 beats per minute, normal intervals, and no ischemic changes. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, and urinary antigens for common bacterial pathogens were collected prior to antibiotics. At the time of this documentation the patient remains seated upright in the emergency department on room air without intravenous fluids, antipyretics, bronchodilators, or vasoactive agents, preserving the physiologic, radiographic, and laboratory data above as his untreated presentation baseline.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age, so 75 years = 75 points. Skilled-nursing facility residence adds 10. Subtotal: 85.
- Comorbidities: cirrhosis adds 20. No malignancy, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, or chronic renal disease: 0 each. Subtotal: 20.
- Examination: respiratory rate 50/min (≥30) adds 20; pulse 126/min (≥125) adds 10. Normal mentation, systolic pressure 106 mm Hg (not <90), and temperature 37.5 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40) add 0 each. Subtotal: 30.
- Labs: arterial pH 7.23 (<7.35) adds 30; BUN 50 mg/dL (≥30) adds 20; sodium 117 mEq/L (<130) adds 20. Glucose 137 mg/dL (not ≥250), hematocrit 60% (not <30%), and PaO₂ 87 mm Hg (not <60) add 0 each. Subtotal: 70.
- Radiograph: right pleural effusion adds 10.
Total = 85 + 20 + 30 + 70 + 10 = 215 (risk class V).
Final answer: 215
